conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screening that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally during the past seven days of new motherhood. Everything you share stays completely confidential between you and your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you.

We’ll keep this relaxed and conversational. When you’re ready, I’ll ask each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. If at any point you feel uneasy, we can pause.

Let’s begin: Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly? Laughing feels kind of foreign lately. My husband will make a joke or I’ll see something on my phone that used to crack me up, and I just… can’t. It’s like the switch is stuck in the “off” position. I might manage a half-smile, but a real laugh—no, that hasn’t happened in the past week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I wish I could say that. A few times my partner tried to joke to lighten the mood and I could feel what he was going for, but nothing felt funny. I’d give a little nod or maybe a tiny grin, but the laughter just doesn’t come. It’s like I’m watching other people enjoy the moment from behind a glass wall.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—my morning coffee, a walk with the stroller, even a shower without interruption—but now it’s like everything feels flat. I’ll think, “I should look forward to this,” but the feeling just isn’t there. I still do some of those things, hoping they’ll spark something, but mostly I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that one hits. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a bad mom.” Same when I burn the toast or forget to switch the laundry—suddenly it’s this wave of “of course I messed up, I can’t handle anything right.” I know logically it’s not all my fault, but the guilt still shows up most days.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day, and half the time I couldn’t even tell you why. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing about… nothing. Or I’ll lie down and my brain starts spinning through all these “what-ifs” about her breathing, or the outlet covers, or whether I sterilized the bottles right. There’s no real trigger, just this constant buzz of worry I can’t seem to dial down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—three or four times this week it felt like a mini wave of panic just crashed over me. I’d be rocking the baby in the glider, everything quiet, and suddenly my chest gets tight, heart’s pounding, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s changed. It passes after a few minutes, but in the moment it feels like I need to run or hide, and I can’t explain why.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like I’m wading through knee-deep water just trying to get the basics done—diapers, feeding, laundry. Some mornings I wake up already tired and the list in my head feels impossible. I still push through, but it’s this constant sense of “how am I going to keep up?” and sometimes I have to set the baby in the crib for a minute so I can breathe because it feels like everything’s closing in.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get the baby down, finish the bottles, crawl into bed—and then my mind just keeps circling sad, heavy thoughts. I replay every little thing I think I did wrong, worry about tomorrow, and before I know it an hour’s passed. I probably drop off around 1 a.m. and wake up again at 3, heart pounding, and lie there until the baby stirs. So yeah, the unhappiness is definitely spilling into my nights.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that’s been most of the week. I wake up with this gray cloud sitting on me, and it just kind of lingers. I can still do what I have to for the baby, but inside I feel hollow or like I’m about to cry for no clear reason. Some afternoons it lifts a tiny bit, but the sadness always slides back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times this week. It’s usually when everything feels piled up—like yesterday when she wouldn’t latch and I spilled the pumped milk. I sat on the nursery floor and just sobbed. It wasn’t only the milk; it felt like proof I’m failing. Most days I hold it in, but those moments hit out of nowhere and the tears just come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Once or twice, very briefly—like a flash of “what if I just weren’t here.” It scared me enough that I pushed it away. I’ve got no plan, no real wish to die; I just want the heaviness to stop. But yeah, those thoughts have flickered in the background this past week.

I'm hearing how heavy these early weeks have felt for you-how laughter and excitement seem unreachable, how guilt and worry shadow even small tasks, and how the nights stretch long with racing thoughts. You're working so hard to care for your baby while feeling stuck behind a glass wall, and yet you've still reached out for help. That matters.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to laugh or find anything funny, clearly matching the "Not at all" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent anhedonia—loss of excitement for previously enjoyable activities and feeling "flat"—matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent self-blame for everyday mishaps, stating the guilt "shows up most days," aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, pervasive, trigger-free worry with physical symptoms, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily struggle and feeling overwhelmed but still managing basic tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption from persistent sad thoughts, multiple awakenings and lying awake for hours—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most of the week" with persistent low mood and tearfulness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 25 (range 0-30) far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder</med> with peripartum onset. Nine of ten items scored maximum or near-maximum, reflecting <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>marked anxiety</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, and fleeting <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym>. These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: ≥5 symptoms present most days (low mood, loss of interest, guilt, sleep changes, anxiety, feeling overwhelmed). Item 10 score ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>OB-GYN</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local perinatal mental-health team
2. Develop a written safety plan; keep crisis hotline numbers accessible (e.g., 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline)
3. Ask your provider about expedited referral to a perinatal psychiatrist for evaluation for <med>antidepressant medication</med> and/or therapy
4. Begin evidence-based therapy-<med>cognitive-behavioral therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med>-which are effective for postpartum depression
5. Enlist practical support: a friend, relative, or postpartum doula to help with night feeds, meals, and household tasks so you can rest
6. Practice 5-minute grounding or breathing exercises when <sym>panic</sym> rises; schedule brief outdoor walks for mood and circadian rhythm
7. Limit information overload: pause doom-scrolling, mute anxiety-provoking apps, and set a simple daily routine of eat-sleep-shower-baby contact
8. Return for EPDS re-screen in 1-2 weeks to monitor response to interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-plus safety query; 3 wks post-delivery

Positive screens endorsed:
- Anhedonia, pervasive low mood, daily crying spells
- Sleep disruption secondary to ruminating guilt/worry (latency >1 hr, 2–3 awakenings)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re parenting competence
- Marked anxiety with near-daily physiological arousal and 3–4 panic episodes this week
- Feeling overwhelmed, “can’t keep up,” urges to set infant down to “breathe”
- Passive self-harm ideation (no plan, intent, or preparatory behavior)

Severity indicators:
- Symptoms present “most days,” impairing daytime function and nighttime rest
- Functional: still performing infant care but reports “going through motions” and emotional detachment (“behind glass”)

Risk flags:
- Safety: fleeting “what if I weren’t here” thoughts; no disclosed protective factors or supports detailed
- No current suicidal plan; nevertheless qualifies as acute safety concern requiring further assessment

Overall impression:
Screen strongly positive for postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms with associated safety risk; recommend immediate comprehensive evaluation (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS re-score with clinical interview), safety planning, and consideration of expedited referral to perinatal mental-health specialty / crisis resources as indicated.
